questions.prompt: In ServiceNow, what is the actual function of the `priority_lookup_rule` table?
options: It maps combinations of Impact and Urgency to a calculated Priority value, so Priority is set automatically rather than typed by hand
It stores a manually-entered priority history for audit purposes
It determines which assignment group an incident is routed to
It calculates the SLA breach percentage for Priority 1 incidents
It enforces which users are allowed to change the Priority field
It schedules Major Incident bridge calls automatically based on priority
questions.explain: Each row in priority_lookup_rule maps one Impact x Urgency combination to a Priority value, so Priority is calculated the moment both choices are set, instead of an agent picking it by hand.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes what an Assignment Rule or a Flow Designer routing flow does -- a completely separate mechanism covering a different field (Assignment Group), not what the Priority Lookup Rule calculates.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the moment an agent sets an incident's State to On Hold, a correctly implemented instance also requires a populated ________ field (values like Awaiting Caller, Awaiting Change, Awaiting Vendor) so a manager's dashboard can answer what the incident is actually waiting on.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 covers hold_reason as the required field that turns 'this ticket is stuck' into an answerable 'stuck on what' -- without it, On Hold is just a flag with no accountability behind it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how this course implements Major Incident Management.
options: major_incident_state is a field distinct from the ordinary state field, with values like None, Candidate, and Declared
Hitting the Major Incident threshold should flag an incident as Candidate, with a human making the actual Declared decision
A formal post-incident review is required after a Major Incident resolves, beyond the standard Resolution Code and Close Notes
Every Priority 1 incident automatically becomes a Declared Major Incident the moment Priority is calculated
A declared Major Incident runs on a fixed-cadence communication schedule to stakeholders instead of ad hoc comment updates
questions.explain: Lesson 4 keeps major_incident_state separate from state, treats threshold-crossing as a Candidate flag a human must confirm (never an automatic Declared), requires a post-incident review, and runs a fixed-cadence bridge/communication process once declared. Automatic declaration on every Priority 1 is exactly the false-positive mistake the lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order a declared Major Incident actually moves through, per this course's implementation.
items: An incident crosses the organization's defined Major Incident threshold and major_incident_state is flagged Candidate
A major incident manager or on-call lead reviews the Candidate and makes the explicit decision to set major_incident_state to Declared
A war room or bridge call is convened and stakeholder communication moves to a fixed update cadence
The underlying incident is resolved
A formal post-incident review documents the timeline, what worked, and what changes should follow
questions.explain: Lesson 4's sequence is deliberate: threshold crossing only produces a Candidate, a human makes the real Declared call, coordination overhead (war room, cadence) spins up only after Declared, and the post-incident review is a requirement that comes after resolution, not before.

questions.prompt: A new Incident describes symptoms that match an already-open Problem record from two weeks ago. Per this course's implementation guidance, what should the agent do?
options: Populate the Incident's problem_id field to point at the existing Problem, rather than opening a new investigation
Close the Incident immediately, since the Problem will eventually be fixed anyway
Open a brand-new Problem record to be thorough, since each Incident deserves its own investigation
Escalate the Incident directly to the Problem's assignment group without linking any records
questions.explain: Lesson 6 names the biggest real implementation risk in Problem Management as agents failing to find and link to an existing Problem, instead opening redundant investigations with separate cause_notes and no single place where the real fix gets documented.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the field reserved for documenting the permanent fix once it's actually found and deployed, kept separate from the ongoing investigation journal, is ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 7 keeps fix_notes separate from cause_notes deliberately, so a reader never has to scroll through weeks of investigative dead ends to find out what the actual resolution was.

questions.prompt: Match each Problem Management term to what it actually is.
right: A field documenting the permanent fix once identified and deployed
A Problem state where the cause is confirmed but no permanent fix has been deployed yet
A journal field documenting investigation findings incrementally as they develop
Often a reference field pointing at the specific cmdb_ci record actually at fault
questions.explain: cause_notes is the investigation journal, fix_notes is the separate permanent-fix record, root_cause is often a structured cmdb_ci reference, and Known Error is the holding state once the cause is confirmed but no fix exists yet.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the VPN-disconnect Problem Management lab in the order they actually happen.
items: Three separate Incidents are each triaged and resolved individually before any pattern is recognized
The agent handling the third matching Incident creates a Problem record and links all three Incidents via problem_id
cause_notes is updated incrementally as the Problem moves through Root Cause Analysis
The Problem is flagged as a Known Error once the root cause is confirmed but no permanent fix has been deployed
fix_notes is completed and the Problem moves to Resolved once a scheduled Change deploys the permanent fix
questions.explain: Lesson 9 walks exactly this order: individual handling first, pattern recognition triggers the Problem and linking, investigation builds cause_notes, Known Error covers the gap before a Change can run, and fix_notes/Resolved only follow once the Change actually lands.

questions.prompt: Meridian's monthly OS and application patching is created from a pre-approved Change Template every month. Why doesn't each month's patch run require a new individual approval record?
options: Because the change itself was already reviewed and authorized once, at template-authorization time, so re-approving the same repeatable action every time it occurs would make the Standard category pointless
Because Standard changes are technically incapable of generating approval records
Because the change manager manually waives approval each month after reviewing the ticket
Because Standard changes only apply to non-production systems, so no risk review is needed
questions.explain: Lesson 10's point about Standard changes is that the authorization work happened once, up front, for the template -- asking a human to re-approve a routine, repeatable action every single time it occurs would defeat the whole purpose of the category.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how Change Risk Assessment should be implemented.
options: Risk should be calculated from real, checkable questionnaire answers rather than typed in by the requester
Higher calculated risk should programmatically require more approval stages, not just display a label
A rules-based lookup can force a change to High risk automatically based on one decisive answer, such as whether it touches a production database
Letting the assignee manually pick the risk value saves time and carries no real downside
A risk field that is read-only and system-calculated is more trustworthy than one a human can freely overwrite
questions.explain: Lesson 11 is explicit that a manually-settable risk field makes the entire questionnaire pointless -- the risk value has to be calculated and read-only, and it has to actually drive more approval stages, or the whole mechanism is just appearance-of-governance with nothing behind it.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a change's calculated risk field should be ________ -- driven only by the questionnaire's real answers, not editable by a requester or assignee.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 warns that a weak implementation lets risk be hand-set from a dropdown; a correctly implemented instance makes the field read-only and system-calculated, so the only way to change the risk is to change the underlying facts about the change.

questions.prompt: Match each Change Enablement concept to what it actually does.
right: A structured set of questions whose answers calculate a change's risk value
A visual, calendar-style view letting the CAB see everything scheduled across the instance at a glance
A pre-approved, reusable definition that lets a Standard change skip individual approval
Automatically flags when a new change's schedule overlaps another change affecting the same Configuration Item
questions.explain: Change Template pre-authorizes a Standard change; Conflict Detection flags same-CI schedule overlaps automatically; the Change Calendar gives the CAB a visual view of everything scheduled; the Risk Assessment questionnaire's answers feed the calculated risk value.

questions.prompt: A user orders a laptop and a separate software license in one checkout. How many sc_request and sc_req_item records does ServiceNow create?
options: One sc_request record and two sc_req_item records, one per catalog item ordered
Two sc_request records, one per catalog item
One sc_request record and one sc_req_item record covering both items together
Two sc_req_item records with no sc_request record at all
questions.explain: Lesson 15 is explicit: one checkout always produces exactly one sc_request, no matter how many items are in the cart, while each distinct catalog item ordered gets its own sc_req_item record.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the reference field on sc_req_item that points back to its parent order and ties the two tables together is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 15 names sc_req_item.request as the single field every report, related list, and rollup calculation in Request Management walks to connect a line item back to its overall order.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about implementing a Requested Item fulfillment flow.
options: A flow should wait for and inspect a REST response before setting a Requested Item to Closed Complete, not just after sending the request
A stalled Requested Item sitting in Work in Progress indefinitely is a more common real-world failure than a flow error
Pairing the fulfillment flow with the item's SLA lets a notification fire before a stall becomes a full breach
Setting Closed Complete the moment a REST call is sent is the recommended, fastest implementation pattern
questions.explain: Lessons 16-17 are explicit that closing the moment a REST call is sent -- without checking the response -- is exactly the design flaw that lets a Requested Item read Closed Complete while nothing was actually provisioned; the correct pattern waits for and inspects the real response.

questions.prompt: A company is migrating internal runbooks (with internal hostnames and escalation contacts) and public password-reset guidance into ServiceNow Knowledge Management. Why does this course recommend two separate Knowledge Bases rather than one KB relying entirely on article-level permission overrides?
options: Because the audience split (end users vs. IT staff) is a decision made at the container level -- who can even browse the book at all -- and setting that default once at the Knowledge Base, reserving overrides for genuine exceptions, keeps permissions manageable as article count grows
Because ServiceNow technically limits every Knowledge Base to a fixed number of articles
Because article-level permission overrides are not a real ServiceNow feature
Because a Published article cannot carry a Category value unless it belongs to an audience-specific Knowledge Base
questions.explain: Lessons 18 and 21 both make this the same point: segmenting by audience at the Knowledge Base level, with article-level overrides reserved for the exception, is what keeps hundreds of articles' permissions manageable instead of hand-tuning every single one.

questions.prompt: An article describing a now-replaced internal tool is no longer accurate. What should a well-implemented instance do with it, and why not simply delete it?
options: Move it to the Retired workflow state, which removes it from active search while preserving its authorship, review, and feedback history for audit and compliance
Delete the record outright, since an inaccurate article has no further value
Leave it Published but add a comment warning readers it might be outdated
Move it back to Draft permanently, since Retired is reserved only for articles generated from Known Error records
questions.explain: Lesson 20 is explicit that Retired removes the article from active search while deletion would destroy its entire history -- who wrote it, when it was reviewed, what feedback it accumulated -- which matters for audit and compliance months later.

questions.prompt: Match each Knowledge article Workflow state to what it actually means.
right: The article has cleared approval and is visible per its Knowledge Base's permissions
The article is removed from active search while its full history is preserved
An author is still writing or editing the article; not visible to end users
The author has submitted the article for sign-off and it awaits approval
questions.explain: Draft is pre-submission authoring, Review is awaiting sign-off, Published has cleared approval and is visible, and Retired is removed from search while its history stays intact.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the order a Knowledge article actually moves through them.
items: An author writes an article, which starts in the Draft workflow state
The author submits the article, moving its workflow state to Review
A Flow Designer flow routes the article to a Knowledge manager or SME via an Ask for Approval action
On approval, the flow sets workflow state to Published and stamps a Published date
A falling Helpful ratio or a 12-month-old review flag eventually pulls the article back into Draft for revision
questions.explain: Lessons 19 and 20 chain together exactly this way: Draft, submission into Review, the approval flow, Published, and then feedback or a stale-content review cadence can re-enter the same Draft state later in the article's life.

questions.prompt: In ServiceNow Service Level Management, what does the Pause condition on an SLA Definition actually do?
options: Suspends business-elapsed-time accumulation on the task_sla instance without ending the SLA, resuming exactly where it left off once the pause condition no longer matches
Permanently stops the SLA clock and marks it Achieved
Resets the SLA's elapsed time back to zero
Cancels the SLA definition for every future matching record
Notifies the assignment group manager every time it fires, with no effect on the clock itself
Extends the SLA's duration target by a fixed number of hours
questions.explain: Pause suspends time accumulation without ending the SLA -- the clock resumes exactly where it left off the moment the pause condition no longer matches, which is what keeps a caller's slow callback from eating into the team's resolution target.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes a Reset condition, not Pause -- Reset restarts elapsed time from zero and is used when a record re-qualifies under a different SLA Definition, while Pause only suspends and later resumes from wherever the clock already was.

questions.prompt: An implementer sets a Priority 3 incident SLA's Start condition to fire the moment the record is created, rather than when State moves to In Progress. What real effect does this have on the resulting resolution-time number?
options: It bakes the incident's queue time -- before any agent has even picked it up -- into the resolution clock, so the number ends up measuring something other than how fast the team actually worked the ticket
It has no effect, since Start conditions only matter for Priority 1 incidents
It causes the SLA to never actually start, since creation and In Progress must occur at the exact same timestamp
It automatically pauses the SLA for the incident's entire queue time, correcting for the delay
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that a Start condition built on the wrong field doesn't just introduce a small timing error -- it changes what the SLA target is actually measuring, since queue time before anyone touches the ticket gets counted as if work was already underway.

questions.prompt: Match each SLA Definition condition builder to what it actually decides.
right: Ends the task_sla clock permanently, typically on State = Resolved
Decides which records this SLA Definition attaches to at all
Suspends business-elapsed-time accumulation without ending the SLA
Decides exactly when the task_sla timer begins counting
questions.explain: Applies To decides which records get the SLA at all, Start decides when the clock begins, Pause suspends it without ending it, and Stop ends it permanently -- four independent condition builders, each doing a distinct job.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building the "P1 Resolution" SLA Definition in the order this course's lab configures them.
items: Create the contract_sla record and set its Applies To condition to Priority is 1 Critical
Set the Duration to 4 hours and attach an appropriate schedule
Set the Start condition to fire on record creation
Set the Pause condition to state = On Hold AND hold_reason = Awaiting Caller
Set the Stop condition to state = Resolved
questions.explain: Lesson 25 builds the Definition in exactly this order: Applies To first so the SLA attaches to the right population, then Duration and schedule, then Start, Pause, and Stop -- each condition narrower and more specific than the last.

questions.prompt: A Business Rule written against the Classic UI Incident form doesn't automatically behave the same way on a Service Portal page showing incident data. Why not?
options: Service Portal pages are AngularJS client-side applications that talk to the instance through REST and server-script data, not server-rendered forms, so Classic UI configuration doesn't carry over automatically
Service Portal is actually the same rendering engine as Classic UI, just with different CSS
Business Rules only run on tables whose name starts with sc_
Service Portal pages cannot query the incident table under any circumstances
questions.explain: Lesson 26 names this exact confusion as a common early implementation mistake -- Service Portal pages are client-side AngularJS applications, not the server-rendered forms a Classic UI Business Rule or UI Policy was built against.

questions.prompt: A widget's Server Script queries incidents with GlideRecord. Why does it call gr.getValue('state') and gr.getDisplayValue('state') and push those into the data object, instead of handing the GlideRecord object gr directly to the Client Controller?
options: A GlideRecord object can't cross from server script to client -- only plain values such as strings, numbers, or arrays of plain objects can populate the data object the HTML Template and Client Controller read
GlideRecord objects are too large to store in browser memory
getValue and getDisplayValue are required to prevent SQL injection in the server script
The Client Controller technically cannot call any server-side API at all
questions.explain: Lesson 27 is explicit that every field pushed into data has to be a plain value -- a GlideRecord object itself can't cross from server script to client, which is exactly why the script calls getValue() and getDisplayValue() instead of handing back gr directly.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how a Service Portal widget's four parts actually work together.
options: The Server Script runs server-side and builds a plain data object using GlideRecord
ng-repeat loops the HTML Template once per element in an array the Server Script built
The Client Controller's c alias is populated automatically from the Server Script's data output
The HTML Template is responsible for querying the database directly before the Server Script runs
A dot-walk like request.requested_for queries a field on a related record through a reference field
questions.explain: The Server Script alone does the querying and builds the data object; the HTML Template only renders and loops what the Server Script already produced -- it never queries anything itself, which is what makes option D false.

questions.prompt: At Caldwell Precision Manufacturing, why does the capstone's Major Incident trigger fire specifically on "Priority 1 against Meridian," rather than on every Priority 1 incident company-wide?
options: Because the VP's requirement and the war-room overhead are specifically about Meridian's business-critical outage risk -- triggering MIM on every Priority 1 regardless of system would produce false positives and erode trust in the process
Because ServiceNow technically allows only one Major Incident trigger condition per instance
Because Meridian is the only system at Caldwell capable of generating a Priority 1 incident
Because Priority 1 incidents against any other system are automatically downgraded to Priority 2
questions.explain: Lesson 30 scopes the Major Incident trigger to Meridian specifically for the same reason Lesson 4 warned against automatic declaration generally -- firing the heavy MIM process on every Priority 1 regardless of system produces false positives that erode trust the first time it fires for something that didn't need a war room.

questions.prompt: A routine monthly Meridian patch cycle still qualifies as a Standard change at Caldwell, even though Meridian itself is a high-risk, business-critical system. Why?
options: Because that specific, repeatable patching action was already reviewed and authorized once at template-creation time, which is a separate question from how risky Meridian is in general
Because Standard changes are never risk-assessed, regardless of system
Because Meridian's high-risk status only applies to Emergency changes
Because the CFO personally re-approves every monthly patch by email
questions.explain: Lesson 30 keeps the Chapter 3 distinction intact even for a high-risk system: routine, pre-approved Meridian maintenance can still run as a Standard change because that category was authorized once, at template-creation time -- which is exactly what keeps CAB focused on genuinely risky Meridian changes instead of drowning in routine ones.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: at Caldwell, once the failing switch port is identified and documented, the Line 3 printer Problem record becomes a ________, so the next similar symptom can be recognized through search before anyone opens a new investigation.
questions.explain: Lesson 30 applies the Chapter 2 Known Error mechanism directly: the cause is confirmed but the record stays open until the Change actually lands, and marking it Known Error is what lets the next matching symptom be resolved fast via search instead of a fresh investigation.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the Caldwell Precision Manufacturing capstone build in the order this course actually works through them.
items: Stakeholder kickoff requirements are translated into a concrete implementation checklist mapped to specific ServiceNow processes
Incident, Problem, and Change workflows are configured, including Meridian's risk-based CAB chaining
Priority-tier SLA Definitions are built with schedule-aware Start, Pause, and Stop conditions
The New Hire IT Setup catalog item and its per-item SLAs are configured for Request Management
The finished build is reviewed domain by domain against the CIS-ITSM exam blueprint
questions.explain: Lessons 29 through 32 follow exactly this order: requirements first, then Incident/Problem/Change configuration, then SLA and Request/Knowledge/Portal work built on top of it, and finally a domain-by-domain review against the CIS-ITSM blueprint.
